Newly emerged first-instar nymphs of the backswimmer Notonecta maculata measure only about 0.25 cm [Lb = about 0.25 cm] in body length, a diminutive size that reflects the limited resources packaged within the egg. Hatching occurs after an incubation period of 17.58 days [ab = 17.58 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a thermal regime typical of late spring ponds in the species' temperate range. At this stage, the dry weight of a neonate is a mere 0.00027 g , underscoring the substantial energetic investment required over the subsequent instars to reach the adult body plan. These initial measurements are critical for understanding the early-life bottlenecks faced by aquatic predators that must secure prey almost immediately after hatching to fuel their rapid development.

Over the course of approximately five nymphal instars, N. maculata undergoes extensive somatic growth, with individuals reaching a maximum body length of 1.6 cm [Li = 1.6 cm] upon the final moult to the imago. This ultimate length is accompanied by a peak dry body mass of 0.03 g , representing more than a hundredfold increase from the neonatal stage and reflecting the accumulation of the chitinous exoskeleton, flight musculature, and fat reserves necessary for overwintering survival. The transition to the winged adult stage marks the completion of structural development, after which no further moulting occurs. Under the same controlled thermal conditions used in the laboratory (20 °C [T = 20 °C]), the entire pre-adult development from egg to imago spans a considerable duration, with the age at first reproduction recorded at 69.96 days after oviposition [tR = 69.96 days after oviposition], a milestone that coincides with the acquisition of functional wings.

Reproductive activity in N. maculata is strongly seasonal, with oviposition concentrated in the autumn months. Females deposit their eggs into plant stems or other substrates, and the typical fecundity during a single reproductive event is a clutch of 60 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 60 eggs]. Under the standard laboratory temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females produce an average of 1 clutch every 14 days [F_R_i = 1 clutch every 14 days], a rapid rate that compensates for the relatively brief autumnal breeding window. Most adults perish over the winter following their reproductive period, making this a semelparous-like life history in which reproductive effort is concentrated into a single, intensive season. The combination of a moderate clutch size with a short inter-clutch interval allows a single female to contribute a substantial number of offspring to the next generation before the onset of winter mortality.

The adult lifespan as an imago in N. maculata is approximately 76.25 days [am = approximately 76.25 days] when individuals are maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a figure that aligns well with the duration of the active summer and early autumn period in many natural populations. This relatively short adult stage places a premium on the rapid acquisition of mates and suitable oviposition sites following the final moult. This synchrony between wing development and reproductive activation is an adaptive feature for a predatory insect that must colonise and exploit temporary pond habitats efficiently before environmental conditions deteriorate.

Comparative studies across congeneric species reveal that the life-history strategy of N. maculata is sculpted by its role as a top invertebrate predator in fishless water bodies. The combination of a low dry weight at birth (0.00027 g)  and a peak adult dry mass of 0.03 g  illustrates a growth trajectory heavily weighted toward the juvenile phase, where rapid size increase enhances both foraging capability and resistance to cannibalism.
